advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a `--version` test that injects a fake `rebar._build_info` with a known COMMIT (and a fixed `importlib.metadata.version`), then asserts the exact output, e.g. `rebar 9.9.9 (abc1234)\n`
evidence: tests/interfaces/facades/test_cli_argparse.py:113: `commit = importlib.import_module("rebar._build_info").COMMIT or "unknown"` (test helper repeats the production lookup)
`.gitignore:107: src/rebar/_build_info.py`: the module is generated at build time and missing from a plain source tree, so both sides fall back to 'unknown'

The repo already injects a fake module this way: tests/unit/test_attestation_signing.py:188-190 `mod = types.ModuleType("rebar._build_info")` ... `monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, "rebar._build_info", mod)`
The only test with a fixed expected value (test_version_flag_without_build_info_or_metadata) covers just the all-missing fallback
advisory.finding: In a source checkout, no unit test checks that the baked `_build_info.COMMIT` actually shows up in the `--version` output. The happy-path tests build their expected value with the same import-and-fallback logic as production. When `_build_info.py` is missing, both sides produce `(unknown)` and the tests pass whether or not production reads COMMIT correctly.
scenarios: Production is changed to read the wrong attribute (e.g. `SHA`) or drops the commit from the format string. On a dev or CI source tree with no `_build_info.py`, both test sides still print `(unknown)` and the unit suite stays green. The bug only surfaces in release.yml's wheel_test, if at all.
advisory.suggested_fix: Add a test that creates `mod = types.ModuleType("rebar._build_info"); mod.COMMIT = "abc1234"`, calls `monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, "rebar._build_info", mod)` and `monkeypatch.setattr(importlib.metadata, "version", lambda name: "9.9.9")`, runs `main(["--version"])`, and asserts `cap.out == "rebar 9.9.9 (abc1234)\n"`. A second case could set `mod.COMMIT = None` and expect `(unknown)`.
